# Daag: Online Gender Violence Archive, Bangladesh

> Before you trust someone, see what they wrote. A verified public record of abusive and victim-blaming comments on gender violence in Bangladesh.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/

## Behind the polite face, read what he wrote.

One comment on its own might mean nothing. A few of them side by side, and you know the man.

Ask first what she was doing outside that late.

You can tell just by looking at what she wore.

Look into her character first.

This news is staged. Do not believe it.

One incident, step by step

### One news story. Four hundred comments. Three are kept.

Easier to show than to tell. Tap through the steps.

- 01 
 The story breaks 
 A woman has been attacked. The press reports it. The post is public. Anyone can read it.

- 02 
 The comments fill up 
 Four hundred within hours. Most are sympathetic. Some are not: blame, abuse, threats.

- 03 
 Someone notices 
 Anyone can send the link and a screenshot without giving their name. It takes two minutes.

- 04 
 A person checks it 
 The link is opened and matched by hand, the screenshot checked for edits. Most submissions are rejected right here.

- 05 
 Three are kept 
 The post may be deleted later. The account may change. But what was written stays on record.

Try to erase it

### Deleting it does not erase it.

Hold the mouse down and rub the line out. However hard you rub, the mark stays. The internet works the same way.

মেয়েটা অত রাতে বাইরে কী করছিল, সেটা আগে জিজ্ঞেস করুন।

#### Check someone. Don’t hunt them.

Everyone has a right to know who they are dealing with. Daag exists for exactly that: one look before you trust someone, hire them, or marry into their family.

But that is where it ends. Do not take these records and brigade someone, circulate their address or phone number, or threaten them. Any such complaint, once proven, means the account is removed.

We hold only comments that were published in the open. Phone numbers, home addresses, private profiles and anything from a closed group never enter this archive.

Anyone who believes a record in their name is wrong can dispute it. The moderator who approved it does not handle the dispute. A different one reviews it within 14 working days.

Emergency helpline

### In danger now? Call. Don’t wait.

Daag keeps records; it cannot come and get you. If someone is threatening you, blackmailing you, or has raised a hand to you, call one of the numbers below without delay. All of them are open day and night, and the calls are free.

# About Daag

> Why this archive exists, what it does and does not record, and the rules it holds itself to.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/about

## Why Daag Exists

In Bangla, দাগ means stain, the kind that does not wash off. The name is deliberate. When men post victim-blaming, misogynistic, or violent commentary on public Facebook posts about gender violence, that behavior should leave a record. This project was built in response to a pattern: when incidents of rape, acid violence, or domestic abuse happen in Bangladesh, the comment sections fill with cruelty and then disappear. Daag exists to make sure they do not.

#### Online cruelty after violence

When news of a rape, acid attack, or domestic violence case spreads on Facebook, the comment sections often become a second site of violence. Victims are blamed for their clothing, behavior, family background, and character. Perpetrators are defended. Survivors are silenced.

These comments disappear quickly. They get moderated, deleted, or buried by newer content. But while they exist, they shape public discourse, discourage survivors from speaking, and signal to perpetrators that their community supports them.

Daag exists to preserve a systematic record of this discourse, not for outrage but for understanding. It is built for researchers, journalists, advocates, and policymakers who need evidence to make the case for change.

#### How Daag Works

Every entry in the Daag archive goes through a structured review process before publication. Submissions are first screened by AI-assisted tools that check for duplicate content, image authenticity, and URL validity. This automated layer reduces the burden on human reviewers and flags potential issues early.

After initial screening, each submission is reviewed by a human moderator who verifies the source, confirms the comment is from a public post, assesses the category and severity, and ensures the submission meets our editorial standards. Moderators can approve, reject, request additional context, or place submissions on hold for further review.

This combination of AI-assisted screening and human editorial judgment allows us to maintain accuracy at scale while ensuring that every published entry has been reviewed by a person who understands the context. No entry is published without human approval.

#### Principles

#### Have questions or feedback?

We welcome inquiries from researchers, journalists, advocates, and anyone interested in the project.

### What people ask

No. Your email and your relationship to the incident are never shown on the site. We keep them only so a moderator can reach you if something is unclear. Your name is never attached to a published entry.

Usually three to five working days, longer when a lot arrives at once. You get a reference number when you submit, and you can use it to check where your report has got to.

It joins a queue. A moderator opens your link, checks whether the screenshot has been edited, settles the category, and then approves it, rejects it, or asks for more. Nothing is published until a person has looked at it.

No. They see the same public entry everyone else sees: their comment, the category, and which incident it was under. They cannot see who submitted it.

They appeal. A different moderator, not the one who approved it, reviews the evidence within 14 working days. If they are right the entry is taken down or corrected, and the reason is recorded.

Any public platform: Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, Reddit. Most submissions come from Facebook because that is where most of this happens in Bangladesh. The one requirement is that the comment is public, so a moderator can open the link and see it too.

# Terms of Use

> The terms that govern use of the Daag archive.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/terms

## Terms of Use

By accessing or using the Daag platform, you agree to the following terms. Please read them carefully.

#### 1. Purpose & Permitted Use

Daag is a civic accountability archive designed for research, journalism, advocacy, public awareness, and informed personal decisions. You may use this platform to search verified entries, submit evidence for review, file appeals, and access aggregated analytics data.

You may **not** use this platform to: harass, threaten, or intimidate any individual; organise or participate in coordinated pile-ons against archived individuals; redistribute archive content for purposes of vigilantism; create derivative platforms or datasets designed to circumvent our moderation safeguards; or scrape, crawl, or bulk-download archive data without express written permission.

#### 2. Submission Responsibilities

By submitting evidence to Daag, you represent and warrant that: the screenshots you upload are genuine and unmanipulated; the URLs you provide link to publicly visible content; you have not fabricated, altered, or deceptively cropped any submitted material; and you are submitting in good faith for purposes consistent with the platform's mission.

You acknowledge that false submissions waste moderator resources, undermine the archive's credibility, and may constitute an offence under applicable laws. Daag reserves the right to permanently restrict submission access and refer evidence of fabrication to relevant authorities.

#### 3. No Verdict / No Guarantee

Daag is a documentation platform, not a court of law. Archive entries represent verified public comments. They do not constitute a legal verdict, criminal finding, or character judgment of any individual.

While we take every reasonable step to verify submissions, we do not guarantee the absolute accuracy of every entry. We encourage users to treat archive data as one input among many in their own judgment. Daag expressly disclaims any representation that an archived entry is sufficient basis for legal, employment, or relationship decisions.

#### 4. Intellectual Property

The Daag platform, including its design, branding, code, and editorial framework, is the intellectual property of the Daag project. Archive entries themselves are derived from publicly visible third-party content and are presented for documentation purposes under fair use / public interest principles.

You may cite, reference, or link to archive entries for journalistic, academic, or advocacy purposes with appropriate attribution. You may not reproduce the platform's design, replicate its database, or create competing services using Daag's data without written authorization.

#### 5. Limitation of Liability

Daag is provided on an "as-is" basis. To the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, the Daag project, its contributors, moderators, and advisors disclaim all warranties, express or implied, including but not limited to implied warranties of merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose, and non-infringement.

In no event shall Daag be liable for any indirect, incidental, special, consequential, or punitive damages arising from your use of the platform, reliance on archive data, or actions taken by third parties based on archived content.

#### 6. Governing Law

These Terms of Use shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of Bangladesh. Any disputes arising from the use of this platform shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Dhaka, Bangladesh.

Daag reserves the right to update these terms at any time. Continued use of the platform following any modification constitutes acceptance of the revised terms. Users will be notified of material changes via a notice on the platform.

# Privacy Policy

> What Daag collects, what it never collects, and how long anything is kept.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/privacy

## Privacy Policy

This policy explains what data we collect, how we use it, and your rights regarding your information on the Daag platform.

#### 1. Information We Collect

When you use Daag, we may collect the following information depending on how you interact with the platform:

**Submissions:** Evidence you submit including screenshots, URLs, context notes, category selections, and optional contact email. **Contact messages:** Your name, email address, subject selection, and message content when you use the contact form. **Search queries:** Aggregate search patterns may be monitored to detect misuse, but individual queries are not stored or linked to identifiable users. **Technical data:** Basic request logs (IP address, browser type, timestamps) maintained by our hosting infrastructure for security purposes.

#### 2. How We Use Your Information

We use collected information for the following purposes: to review and moderate evidence submissions; to respond to contact form messages and support requests; to process and resolve appeals; to maintain platform security and prevent abuse; to generate anonymised, aggregate analytics displayed publicly on the platform; and to improve the accuracy and reliability of the archive.

We do **not** use your information for advertising, marketing to third parties, or any purpose unrelated to the platform's civic accountability mission.

#### 3. Data Retention

Different types of data are retained for different periods:

**Contact emails:** Messages submitted through the contact form are retained for 180 days, after which they are permanently deleted unless they relate to an ongoing matter. **Submissions:** Approved submissions are retained permanently as part of the public archive for as long as they remain published. Rejected or withdrawn submissions are deleted within 90 days. **Appeals:** Appeal records, including supporting evidence and reviewer notes, are retained for 2 years from the date of resolution. **Technical logs:** Server logs are automatically purged after 30 days.

#### 4. Data Sharing

Your personal information is accessible only to authorised Daag moderators who need it to perform their moderation duties. We do **not** sell, rent, or share your personal data with any third party.

Approved archive entries (which contain public Facebook comments, not private data) are visible to all platform users by design. Submitter contact information is never displayed publicly. We may disclose information if required by law or to protect the safety of individuals, but we will resist overbroad requests and notify affected users where legally permitted.

To run the platform we rely on a small number of service providers who process data on our behalf and under our instructions: **Supabase** hosts the database and the evidence files, **Vercel** serves the website, and **Formspree** delivers messages sent through the contact form to our mailbox. Using the contact form means your name, email address and message pass through Formspree. If you would rather not, write to us directly at [daagarchive@gmail.com](mailto:daagarchive@gmail.com).

#### 5. Screenshots & Evidence

Screenshots submitted as evidence are stored securely and reviewed by our moderation team before publication. All submitted media is verified for authenticity. Screenshots of public Facebook comments are published as part of approved archive entries.

We do not accept or publish screenshots containing private messages, closed-group content, or any material not from publicly visible posts. If a screenshot is found to contain personal information beyond the public comment (such as phone numbers or addresses visible in the background), that information will be redacted before publication.

#### 6. Cookies & Tracking

Daag uses Supabase for backend services, which may set functional cookies necessary for the platform to operate (such as session management). We also use **Google Analytics (GA4)** to collect anonymous, aggregated website usage data (such as page views, session duration, and general geographic region) to help us understand how visitors interact with the platform and improve the user experience.

Google Analytics may set cookies to distinguish unique users and sessions. No personally identifiable information is collected or shared through Google Analytics. We do **not** use third-party advertising trackers or social media pixels. The submission-related analytics displayed on our platform are computed entirely from our own database. For more information on how Google processes data, visit [Google's Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy).

#### 7. Your Rights

You have the right to: **Access** any personal data we hold about you; **Correction** of inaccurate personal information; **Deletion** of your personal data (such as contact form messages or submitter email addresses); and **Objection** to processing of your data in certain circumstances.

To exercise any of these rights, please submit a request through our [contact page](/contact). We will respond to all legitimate requests within 30 days. Note that deletion requests regarding approved archive entries (which document public comments) will be handled through the formal [appeals process](/appeals).

#### 8. Children's Privacy

Daag is not intended for use by individuals under the age of 16. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children. If we become aware that we have inadvertently collected data from a child under 16, we will take steps to delete that information promptly.

If you believe a child has submitted personal information to Daag, please [contact us](/contact) immediately so we can address the situation.

#### 9. Changes to This Policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time to reflect changes in our practices, technology, or legal requirements. When we make material changes, we will post a notice on the platform and update the "Last updated" date below.

Continued use of the platform after changes are posted constitutes acceptance of the revised policy. We encourage you to review this page periodically.

#### 10. Contact Us

If you have questions about this Privacy Policy, wish to exercise your data rights, or have concerns about how your information is handled, please reach out through our [contact page](/contact).

We take all privacy inquiries seriously and will respond as promptly as possible.

# 180 days in the law, three and a half years in practice

> Bangladesh's Women and Children Repression Prevention Act gives tribunals 180 working days to finish a case. Research presented in Dhaka puts the real average at three years and seven months. Here is what October's verdicts show.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/180-days-in-law-three-years-in-practice

Bangladesh's Women and Children Repression Prevention Act, 2000 requires a tribunal to finish a case within 180 working days. Research presented at the BRAC Centre in Dhaka found that a case actually takes an average of **three years and seven months**, across an average of twenty-two hearing dates ([Prothom Alo, 2 May 2026](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/ebsz0axkin)).

That single gap explains most of what people mean when they say the system does not work. It is also why so many women are told, by the people closest to them, that there is no point starting.

October 2026 happened to produce a set of verdicts that show the spread unusually clearly.

## What the courts decided in October

Four judgments reported in the second half of the month, with the time from offence to verdict:

| Verdict | Reported | Offence dated | Elapsed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three men jailed for life for a gang rape on a moving bus in Tangail, fined Tk 2 lakh each | [25 Oct 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/3-get-life-gang-raping-woman-moving-bus-tangail-4307206) | 14 January 2026 | about 9 months |
| An imam jailed for life in Jamalpur for raping a 15-year-old student | [26 Oct 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/imam-gets-life-term-over-rape-girl-4307536) | November and December 2020 | about 6 years |
| A man jailed for life in Gopalganj for raping a 15-year-old girl | [15 Oct 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/man-gets-life-sentence-raping-15-year-old-girl-gopalganj-4299456) | 16 December 2023 | about 3 years |

All three ended in conviction. All three were reported within eleven days of each other. And the distance between them, nine months against six years, is the thing worth paying attention to.

For comparison, in July a tribunal in Mymensingh delivered three death sentences **twenty-five days** after the incident ([Prothom Alo, 9 July 2026](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/district/io0nn0q3wi)).

Twenty-five days and six years are both real outcomes under the same statute.

## The 180 days is a direction, not a deadline

There is a legal reason the clock slips, and it is not widely discussed.

Section 20 of the Act says a tribunal shall complete a trial within 180 days of receiving the case. Section 31A says that if it does not, the tribunal must record the reasons and file a report with the Supreme Court within thirty days.

In September 2026 the High Court held that the 180-day provision is **directory, not mandatory**: a trial that runs past it is not void, and the delay does not by itself entitle an accused to have proceedings quashed. The ruling came in a petition filed back in 2011 by an accused seeking exactly that, on the grounds that the deadline had passed and no report had been filed ([Prothom Alo, 23 September 2026](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/7ilfivbbpy)).

The practical effect is worth stating plainly. The deadline is real, the reporting duty is real, and neither carries a consequence that stops a case from drifting. A tribunal that misses 180 days files a reason. A tribunal that files a reason carries on.

That is how a statute can promise six months and deliver three and a half years without anyone breaking it.

## Why the fast ones are fast

A case that finishes quickly is usually a case where three things happened to line up: the accused was arrested early, the medical and forensic evidence was collected while it still existed, and the witnesses stayed reachable and willing.

None of those are guaranteed by the law. They are guaranteed by circumstance.

The Mymensingh case moved in twenty-five days because the accused were in custody and the evidence was fresh. The Jamalpur case took six years because, as the prosecution described it, the offences dated to late 2020 and the case had to travel the full distance of an ordinary tribunal docket.

The law's 180-day clock does not start the engine. It only tells you how far behind schedule the engine already is.

## What happens to the rest

The same research puts the conviction rate in cases under the Act at **3 percent**, with roughly **70 percent** of defendants acquitted.

A 70 percent acquittal rate is not evidence that 70 percent of complaints were untrue. It is mostly evidence of what three and a half years does to a case: witnesses move, memories blur, physical evidence degrades or was never collected properly, and families under pressure settle or stop attending. Several of those are failures of investigation, not of the complaint.

The Daily Star followed one case through to its end: a twenty-year fight that closed in July 2025 with the accused acquitted for insufficient evidence ([25 September 2025](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/justice-eludes-women-children-trials-drag-3995001)).

Twenty years is not a trial. It is a sentence served by the complainant.

## The false-case verdict, and what it does not prove

On 13 October a Netrokona tribunal sentenced a woman to one year of rigorous imprisonment and a Tk 5,000 fine for filing a false rape case. The case she had filed dated to 2008 ([The Daily Star, 13 Oct 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/netrokona-woman-jailed-filing-false-rape-case-4297881); [Prothom Alo, 14 Oct 2026](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/district/vda9kiabbr)).

That verdict is a real finding by a court and it deserves to be reported accurately. It also gets used, within hours of publication, to argue something it does not support.

Two things are worth separating:

1. **A court found this particular complaint false.** That is what the judgment says.
2. **An acquittal is not a finding that a complaint was false.** Those are different legal conclusions, reached by different standards. Conflating them turns a 70 percent acquittal rate into a 70 percent lying rate, which is not what the number means and not what any court has found.

The distance between those two sentences is where most of the comment section lives.

## What this means if you are deciding whether to report

Nothing above is an argument against filing. It is an argument for knowing the shape of the thing you are starting.

- **The clock in the statute is not the clock you will experience.** Plan for years, not months, unless the accused is arrested immediately.
- **Evidence collected in the first days decides most of it.** Medical examination, the scene, the phone, the screenshots. What is not collected early is usually not recoverable later.
- **Keep your own copies of everything**, including anything posted publicly about the case. Posts get deleted. Screenshots do not.
- **The reference number matters.** Whatever you file, keep the number and the date. It is how you find out where the case has got to without depending on anyone's memory.

## Where Daag fits

Daag does not investigate incidents and does not take a position on guilt in any criminal matter. It records something narrower and specific: [what gets written publicly](/archive) underneath reporting about these cases.

When a verdict like October's is published, a predictable second event follows in the comments. That second event is the thing this archive keeps, with a screenshot, a link to the source post, and a category, reviewed by a person before anything is published. You can [read the record](/archive), [search a name or profile](/search), or [submit a comment you have seen](/submit).

If an entry about you is wrong, [the appeals process](/appeals) is reviewed by a moderator other than the one who approved it.

---

**Sources.** Every figure above links to the report it came from. The three October verdicts are from The Daily Star's crime and justice desk; the conviction rate, the 180-day provision and the three-years-seven-months average are from Prothom Alo's report on research presented at the BRAC Centre on 2 May 2026. Dates are the publishers' own.

*Daag is a public archive, not a law firm. Nothing here is legal advice. For urgent help call 999, or 109 for the national women and children helpline.*

# Nineteen days: what Bangladesh's fastest trial actually required

> A Dhaka tribunal convicted two people nineteen days after an eight-year-old was killed in Pallabi. Five hearings, sixteen witnesses. Here is what made it possible, and why the case is not over.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/nineteen-days-what-the-fastest-trial-required

On 19 May 2026 an eight-year-old girl was killed in Pallabi, Dhaka, after being raped. On 7 June, nineteen days later, a tribunal sentenced two people to death for it. The Law Minister called it the fastest trial in Bangladesh's history ([The Daily Star, 7 June 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/ramisa-murder-sohel-wife-swapna-sentenced-death-4192556)).

Set that against the average. Research presented at the BRAC Centre in Dhaka found that a case under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act takes an average of **three years and seven months**, across twenty-two hearing dates ([Prothom Alo, 2 May 2026](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/ebsz0axkin)).

Nineteen days against three and a half years is not a small difference. It is worth understanding exactly what produced it, because the answer is less encouraging than the headline.

**A note on naming.** This case is universally reported under the child's name. Daag does not repeat the names of children who were raped or killed, including where the press has published them. Section 14 of the Act restricts identifying victims, and an archive built around how people are spoken about publicly should hold itself to that even when others do not. The case is referred to here by where it happened.

## What the record shows

| | |
|---|---|
| Incident | 19 May 2026, Pallabi, Dhaka |
| Verdict | 7 June 2026 |
| Elapsed | 19 days |
| Hearings | 5 |
| Prosecution witnesses | 16 |
| Sentence | Death for both accused, aged 31 and 26 |
| Fines | Tk 5 lakh and Tk 2 lakh, ordered paid to the victim's legal heirs |

The judge was Masrur Salekin of the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal in Dhaka Metropolitan, who wrapped up proceedings in five hearings ([The Daily Star, 5 June 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/ramisa-murder-verdict-sunday-after-19-days-4191026)). The sixteen witnesses included the child's parents and elder sister, three neighbours, a doctor, a magistrate and the investigating officer.

The detail worth pausing on is the fine. The tribunal ordered it paid to the victim's legal heirs, which is a form of redress the Act allows and which almost never gets reported.

## What made it fast

Four things happened here that do not usually happen together.

**The accused were in custody immediately.** Nothing in a tribunal can move while the accused is absconding. A warrant that cannot be executed is the single most common reason a case sits still for years.

**The evidence was fresh.** Medical and forensic evidence in a rape case degrades on a timescale of days. When the examination happens at once and the scene is preserved, the prosecution has something to put in front of a judge. When it happens weeks later, often it does not.

**The witnesses were available and willing.** Sixteen witnesses across five hearings means nobody had to be summoned repeatedly. In an ordinary case, the average of twenty-two hearing dates is largely a record of witnesses who did not come.

**The state wanted it.** There was national outrage, and the government publicly committed to a fast trial.

Only the first three are things the justice system controls. The fourth is the one that decided this case, and it is not available to most complainants. A case becomes fast when it becomes politically costly to be slow.

## Why the case is not over

The reporting mostly stopped at the verdict. Two days later something procedural but important happened: the death reference was sent to the Supreme Court ([The Daily Star, 9 June 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/ramisa-rape-murder-death-reference-sent-supreme-court-4194481)).

A death reference is mandatory. A death sentence passed by a trial court has no effect until the High Court Division confirms it. The convicts may also appeal. So the nineteen-day figure describes the trial court stage only, and the final outcome is not yet known.

This matters for how the case gets discussed. A sentence that is pending confirmation is routinely described online as settled, final and carried out. It is none of those things yet.

## What the comments did with it

This is the part Daag records.

A case this fast, this public and this severe produces a very particular reaction underneath the reporting. Some of it is grief. A large share of it is something else: demands for extrajudicial punishment, arguments that trials are a waste of time, and, within a day, the familiar pivot to what the child's family should have done differently.

That last move is the one worth noticing, because an eight-year-old leaves almost no room for it. The reasoning does not stop when the victim is a child; it relocates to the mother, to the neighbourhood, to the family's circumstances.

[The archive](/archive) exists to keep that second record. Not the crime, which the courts and the press handle, but what named people wrote publicly underneath it, with a screenshot and a link to the source post, reviewed by a person before publication.

## The honest conclusion

Nineteen days proves the system can move. It does not prove the system does move.

Everything that made this case fast was circumstantial: an immediate arrest, intact evidence, willing witnesses, and sustained public attention. Strip out the public attention and you have an ordinary case, and [the ordinary case takes three and a half years](/blog/180-days-in-law-three-years-in-practice) if it survives at all.

The useful question after a verdict like this one is not whether justice is possible. It is why the conditions for it have to be exceptional.

---

**Sources.** The Daily Star's crime and justice desk for the verdict, the five hearings and the death reference; Prothom Alo for the research on average case duration. Dates and figures are the publishers' own, and each links to the report it came from.

*Daag is a public archive, not a law firm, and nothing here is legal advice. If you are in danger now, call 999. For the national women and children helpline, call 109.*

# A harassment video went viral. Then the question became who gets detained.

> A woman was assaulted on a Dhanmondi footpath in daylight with a police officer present. What happened next, and what the comment section did with it.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/the-footpath-video-and-who-gets-detained

Around midday on a Monday in October, a woman was assaulted on the footpath opposite Bangladesh Eye Hospital on Satmasjid Road in Dhanmondi. An assistant sub-inspector was present at the scene. He was later withdrawn from his post over allegations of negligence of duty ([Prothom Alo, 14 October 2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/crime-and-law/5ks378n363)).

Video of the incident circulated widely. What followed is the part worth setting out carefully, because it was widely described online in a way the reporting does not support.

## What actually happened, in order

The sequence matters, so here it is as reported:

1. A woman was harassed in public, in daylight, with a police officer present who did not intervene.
2. She contacted a relative.
3. The relative confronted the man accused of harassing her and assaulted him.
4. **The relative was detained and sentenced to 15 days in jail.**
5. The officer who had been present was withdrawn from his post for negligence.
6. Separately, a young man was detained over the footpath assault and produced before a metropolitan magistrate.

Police also said the man accused of the harassment suffers from a mental illness.

The woman's own description of where this left her, in a written statement she sent to Prothom Alo and also posted on social media, was a question: "Then are we the ones who have committed a crime by trying to protect myself?" ([Prothom Alo, 15 October 2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/city/solae1k2ja)).

## Being accurate about it

The version that travelled fastest online was that a woman was jailed for defending herself. That is not what happened, and repeating it does the case no favours.

The person jailed was a relative, and what he was jailed for was assaulting someone. Those are real facts and they matter, both to him and to the man he assaulted, who police say is mentally ill.

What is also true, and is the thing the woman's question actually points at, is the shape of the outcome: the harassment produced no immediate consequence for anyone, the officer who watched it produced a transfer, and the only custodial sentence in the first days went to the person who intervened.

You do not have to believe the relative should have escaped consequences to notice that ordering. A system can be applying the law correctly in each individual step and still produce a sequence that teaches women not to expect protection.

## The vicarious lesson

This is the mechanism that makes incidents like this one matter beyond the people involved.

Most women will never be assaulted on Satmasjid Road. Nearly all of them will see the video and read the comments, and will take from it a conclusion about what happens if they ask for help in public. That conclusion is formed long before anyone reaches a police station, and it is formed by the reaction as much as by the event.

Prothom Alo has reported on women facing security risks amid both mob violence and online attacks ([8 January 2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/io0fojls6x)), and The Daily Star has called online abuse a national crisis ([8 March 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/supplements/international-womens-day-2026/news/online-abuse-now-national-crisis-time-act-4122986)).

Of everyone recorded as a victim of cyber violence in Bangladesh in the first half of 2025, **97 percent were women and children**, according to a platform convened by the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust with fourteen organisations ([Prothom Alo, 9 July 2025](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/7gdiyso4ho)).

## What the comments did

A video like this produces a predictable split, and both halves are documented in [this archive](/archive).

- **What was she doing there.** Applied to a public footpath at midday, which is roughly the safest set of circumstances available, and still applied.
- **It is staged.** The claim that the video is arranged, that the woman is an actor, or that the whole thing is a campaign. This survives the presence of a police officer and a magistrate.
- **She should be grateful.** Directed at a woman who said she did not feel protected.
- **Sympathy that turns into a demand.** Support for the woman, followed quickly by instructions about how she should now behave, dress, or travel.

Daag does not record these because the opinions are forbidden. It records them because they are public statements by named accounts, they shape what the next woman expects, and they are routinely deleted once a story stops trending.

## If you see something like this

The practical version, for anyone who wants the record to survive:

- **Capture the comment, not just the video.** The video will be reposted by many accounts. The comment, with its author, usually exists in one place and gets removed.
- **Include the source post link.** A screenshot with no link cannot be verified, and an entry that cannot be verified does not get published here.
- **Do not edit the image.** No cropping out the timestamp, no highlighting. An altered screenshot is not evidence.
- **Act while it is public.** Deleted comments cannot be checked against their source.

The full standard is on the [about page](/about), and you can [submit](/submit) what you have.

---

**Sources.** Prothom Alo for the incident, the officer's withdrawal, the detention and the woman's statement; The Daily Star and Prothom Alo for the context on online abuse. Each figure links to the report it came from.

*Daag is a public archive, not a law firm, and nothing here is legal advice. If you are in danger now, call 999. For the national women and children helpline, call 109. For online harassment and blackmail, Police Cyber Support for Women is on 01320-000888.*

# The vocabulary of blame: the phrases that come back every time

> Across the comments this archive records, the same small set of moves repeats. Naming them is the first step to recognising them, and to documenting them properly.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/the-vocabulary-of-blame

A Bangladeshi woman who was harassed while shopping with her parents at Meradia Bazar in Banasree described her experience to Prothom Alo under a headline that is itself the summary: "Everything seems to be women's fault" ([10 May 2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/p4vwsoje02)).

By her account, a man had been staring at her for a long time. She asked him what he was looking at. He became aggressive.

That exchange, and what follows it in public, is the subject of this archive. Not the staring and not the aggression, which are matters for other institutions, but the second event: what gets written afterwards by people who were not there.

Across the entries Daag has published, the same small set of moves comes back. They are worth naming, because a pattern you can name is a pattern you can recognise in the first second rather than the tenth.

## The moves

**Relocating the question.** The subject changes from what was done to what she should not have done. Why was she out, why that route, why that hour, why answer back. The grammar of the sentence stays about the incident while the subject quietly becomes the woman.

This is the single most common move in the archive, and it is the reason the category exists at all.

**Attacking the delay.** Why did she wait, why speak now, why not go to the police that night. The question is never applied in reverse: nobody asks why an investigation took three years. The [average case under the Act takes three years and seven months](/blog/180-days-in-law-three-years-in-practice), which is a fact about the system that is routinely held against the person reporting.

**Disputing the record.** The screenshot is edited, the video is staged, the press is selling something, the whole thing is a campaign. This one is notable because it survives evidence. It survives a conviction, a confession, and a police officer standing in the frame.

**Appearance as explanation.** What she was wearing, offered as if it were an account of someone else's conduct.

**Generalising from a single case.** One false-case verdict becomes a statement about all complaints. We have written separately about [why an acquittal is not a finding that a complaint was false](/blog/what-the-comments-do-after-a-verdict), because that conflation does most of the work here.

**Religious or moral framing.** The incident becomes an illustration of social decline, with the woman as the illustration.

**Threats and address-hunting.** Rarer, and categorically different. At the point where a comment moves from opinion about a story to locating a person, it stops being speech about an event and becomes preparation for one.

## Why naming them matters

Two reasons, one practical and one not.

The practical one: Daag categorises every published entry, and the categories are these moves. A submission arrives, a moderator reads it, and part of the review is deciding which of these it is. Knowing the vocabulary makes a submission easier to assess and faster to process. You can see the [distribution across the archive](/analytics).

The other reason is that these phrases are load-bearing. They are not decoration on top of the violence; they are part of the machinery that decides whether a woman reports at all. ActionAid found that **85 percent** of women who experienced online violence never complained to anyone ([Prothom Alo, 27 November 2022](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/p5uqt9qjl3)). A woman reading the comments under someone else's case is being told, in advance and at scale, what would be said about hers.

## What this archive does and does not claim

It is worth being precise, because the distinction is easy to lose.

| | |
|---|---|
| Daag records | What a named account wrote publicly, with a screenshot and a source link |
| Daag does not record | Private messages, deleted content it cannot verify, or anything it cannot open and check |
| Daag does not claim | That a comment is a crime, or that its author committed any offence |
| Daag does not take a position | On guilt in any criminal matter the comment refers to |

Holding an ugly opinion in public is not an offence, and this archive does not treat it as one. What it does is remove the assumption that a public statement disappears when its author would prefer it to.

That is the whole mechanism. The comment was already public. The only thing Daag adds is durability.

## Documenting one properly

If you want to record something of this kind so that it holds:

1. **Screenshot the comment with its author visible**, and enough of the thread around it to show what it was replying to. A crop of the words alone cannot be assessed.
2. **Copy the link to the source post**, so a moderator can open it.
3. **Copy the link to the commenter's profile.** Names repeat; profiles do not.
4. **Do not edit the image** in any way, including highlighting.
5. **Transcribe it if you can.** Optional, and it is what makes the entry findable in a search later.

Then [submit it](/submit). Nothing is published automatically; a moderator checks the links and the screenshot first, usually within three to five working days, and you get a reference number to track it.

Anyone named in a published entry can [appeal](/appeals), and a different moderator reviews it within fourteen working days.

---

**Sources.** Prothom Alo for the Banasree account and the ActionAid research. The categories described here are Daag's own, derived from the entries in [the archive](/archive) and visible in the [analysis](/analytics).

*Daag is a record, not a verdict and not a punishment. If you are in danger now, call 999. For the national women and children helpline, call 109.*

# What a confession in court does not settle

> A driver confessed to the rape and murder of a schoolgirl in Cumilla. Prothom Alo then listed the questions the confession leaves open. Here is what a section 164 statement is, and what it is not.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/what-a-confession-does-not-settle

In October a CNG-run auto-rickshaw driver gave a confessional statement to a magistrate in Cumilla, admitting to the rape and murder of a 15-year-old schoolgirl whose body was found in a paddy field in Lalmai ([The Daily Star, 11 October 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/cng-driver-confesses-rape-murder-schoolgirl-4295571)).

For most readers, that is where the story ends. A man confessed. It is solved.

On the same day, Prothom Alo published a piece titled "Many questions remain unanswered" ([11 October 2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/local-news/shxvqywpcb)).

Both are accurate. Understanding why is useful, and not only for this case.

*As with other cases involving children, this piece does not repeat the victim's name, though it has been widely published.*

## What is known

Police said the girl hired the driver's auto-rickshaw from Paduar Bazar to Racecourse for Tk 300 at around 12:30am. The driver was arrested at his brother's house in Chattogram, and police recovered the phone taken from the girl's bag from a location he identified ([The Daily Star, 10 October 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/driver-arrested-over-murder-cumilla-girl-4294736)).

The confession was given before a Senior Judicial Magistrate in Cumilla.

## What the confession does not answer

Prothom Alo's follow-up set out the gaps plainly. Two stand out:

- **The route.** The destination was about eight kilometres away. The body was found after what the reporting describes as a roughly thirty-kilometre detour, in the opposite direction from the city.
- **Whether anyone else was involved**, which the investigation had not resolved.

There is a further point in that report worth repeating: the girl's family had lived in Cumilla for years, so she would have had some familiarity with the local geography. A thirty-kilometre detour in the wrong direction is not obviously something a local passenger fails to notice.

None of this means the confession is false. It means a confession is a piece of evidence, not a conclusion.

## What a section 164 statement actually is

In Bangladeshi criminal procedure, a confessional statement recorded by a magistrate under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a formal, recorded admission. The magistrate is required to satisfy himself that it is voluntary and to warn the person that it may be used against him.

Three things follow that are routinely missed in public discussion:

| | |
|---|---|
| A confession can be **retracted** | Retracted confessions are common, and a court must then decide what weight to give it |
| A confession usually needs **corroboration** | Courts are cautious about convicting on a retracted confession alone, without supporting evidence |
| A confession binds **the person who made it** | It is not, by itself, evidence against a co-accused |

That third point is why the open question about whether anyone else was involved matters. If the investigation closes on the confession, any other participant becomes materially harder to charge later.

## Why this gets flattened online

The gap between "a man confessed" and "the investigation has unanswered questions" is where a lot of public argument happens, in both directions.

One side treats the confession as the end: the case is closed, further questions are an insult to the victim, and anyone raising them is making excuses. The other treats the unanswered questions as proof the whole thing is staged.

Neither follows. An investigation can produce a real confession and still be incomplete. Saying so is not scepticism about the victim; it is the ordinary condition of a case that is still being investigated.

Daag records the public reaction to cases like this one, not the case itself. The reaction worth recording here is not the argument about the route. It is the reliable arrival, within hours of any report involving a girl out at night, of comments about what she was doing in an auto-rickshaw at half past midnight.

That question is directed at a dead child. It is also, in the pattern this archive documents, one of the three or four most common responses to this category of story.

## For anyone following a case

A few things make it easier to follow reporting on a criminal case without being misled:

1. **Separate the stages.** Arrest, confession, charge framing, trial, verdict, and appeal are different events. Reporting on one is routinely read as the conclusion of all of them.
2. **Note who is speaking.** "Police said" is not a finding of fact. A press briefing describes an allegation at that moment in an investigation.
3. **Watch for the retraction.** It is common and it is rarely reported with the same prominence as the confession.
4. **A death sentence is not final at the trial court.** It goes to the High Court Division for confirmation, as happened in [the Pallabi case](/blog/nineteen-days-what-the-fastest-trial-required).
5. **Screenshot what you want to keep.** Reporting is edited and comment threads are deleted. If you intend to cite something later, capture it now.

## Where Daag fits

The archive does not investigate incidents, take a position on guilt, or publish anything about a case that a court has not. What it keeps is narrower: [what named people wrote publicly](/archive) underneath the reporting, with a screenshot and a source link, checked by a moderator before anything is published.

If you have seen something of that kind, you can [submit it](/submit). If an entry about you is wrong, [the appeals process](/appeals) is handled by a moderator other than the one who approved it.

---

**Sources.** The Daily Star's crime and justice desk for the arrest and the confession; Prothom Alo for the open questions in the investigation. The description of section 164 is a general statement of Bangladeshi criminal procedure, not advice on this case or any other.

*Daag is a public archive, not a law firm. For urgent help call 999, or 109 for the national women and children helpline.*

# What the comment section does after a verdict

> When a Bangladeshi court convicts someone of rape, a second, predictable event happens underneath the reporting. Here is the pattern, what the data says, and how to document it.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/what-the-comments-do-after-a-verdict

A verdict gets published. Within a few hours, underneath it, a second thing happens that is not reporting and is not justice. It is a comment section, and it follows a shape regular enough to predict.

This archive exists because that second thing is a public act by a named person, and because it disappears when someone decides it should.

## The shape it takes

Across the entries in [this archive](/archive), the same handful of moves come up again and again under reporting about gender violence:

- **Relocating the question to the woman.** What was she doing out, what was she wearing, why was she there at that hour. The subject quietly changes from what the accused did to what she should not have done.
- **Attacking the delay.** Why did she wait, why now, why did she not go to the police the same night. The three-and-a-half-year average a case actually takes is never applied to the question of why anyone hesitates.
- **Disputing the record itself.** The screenshots are edited, the story is arranged, the press is selling something. This one survives even a conviction.
- **Generalising from one case.** A single false-case verdict becomes proof about every complaint ever filed.
- **Threats and address-hunting.** Less frequent, far more serious, and the point at which a comment stops being speech about a story and becomes a plan.

None of those are rare. They are the ordinary weather of a Bangladeshi comment section after this kind of story.

## What the data says about who gets hit

Of everyone recorded as a victim of cyber violence in Bangladesh in the first six months of 2025, **97 percent were women and children**. The figure comes from a platform convened by the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust with fourteen organisations including BRAC, Naripokkho, Bangladesh Mahila Parishad and Ain o Salish Kendra, analysing 29 documented incidents ([Prothom Alo, 9 July 2025](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/7gdiyso4ho)).

Separately, ActionAid found that about **64 percent** of women online had faced violence there, up fourteen percentage points on the year before, and that **85 percent of them never complained to anyone** ([Prothom Alo, 27 November 2022](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/p5uqt9qjl3)).

That last number is the one that matters most for anyone deciding whether documentation is worth the trouble. The overwhelming majority of this is never reported to anyone at all, which means the official record of online abuse in Bangladesh is a small sample of a much larger thing.

The Daily Star has called online abuse a national crisis and argued the legal framework has not kept up ([8 March 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/supplements/international-womens-day-2026/news/online-abuse-now-national-crisis-time-act-4122986)), and documented the specific gaps in law and enforcement that let cyber violence against women continue ([17 December 2025](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/gaps-laws-enforcement-fuel-cyber-violence-against-women-4061176)).

## The one that needs care

In October a Netrokona tribunal convicted a woman of filing a false rape case, in a matter dating back to 2008 ([The Daily Star, 13 October 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/netrokona-woman-jailed-filing-false-rape-case-4297881)).

That is a real judgment and it should be reported as one. Within hours it also becomes the single most reused argument in comment sections: proof, supposedly, that complaints in general cannot be trusted.

It is worth being precise about what it does and does not establish, because the imprecision is the whole point of the reuse:

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| A court found **this** complaint false | What the judgment says |
| Acquittal means the complaint was false | **No.** Different legal conclusions, different standards of proof |
| A 70 percent acquittal rate means 70 percent lied | **No.** No court has found that, and the research attributes acquittals largely to delay and evidentiary failure |

Conviction for a false case is a specific finding, reached after a separate trial. Treating it as a statement about complainants generally is not a reading of the judgment. It is a use of it.

Daag records that use when it happens publicly under someone's real name. Not because the opinion is forbidden, but because it is a public act with an author, and the authorship is what tends to vanish.

## How to document a comment properly

If you are going to record something, record it so it holds up. The archive's own standard, and the reason entries get rejected:

1. **Capture the comment before anything else.** Full screenshot, showing the comment, the account name, and enough of the surrounding thread that context is visible. Not a crop of the words alone.
2. **Copy the link to the source post**, not just the comment. The post is what lets a moderator open it and check.
3. **Copy the link to the commenter's profile.** A display name is not an identifier; two people share a name, a profile does not.
4. **Do not edit the image.** Not to highlight, not to blur, not to crop out the timestamp. An edited screenshot cannot be verified and will be rejected.
5. **Type the comment out if you can.** The screenshot is the proof; the transcription is what makes it findable in a search later. It is optional, and an entry without it is still valid.
6. **Record it while it is public.** A comment that has been deleted cannot be verified against its source, and an entry that cannot be verified does not get published.

The requirement that trips most submissions is the second one. A screenshot with no source link is a picture of text, and a picture of text is not evidence of who wrote it.

## What happens after you submit

Nothing is published automatically. A submission goes into a queue, a moderator opens the links, checks whether the screenshot has been altered, settles the category, and then approves, rejects, or asks for more. Typical turnaround is three to five working days, and you get a reference number to check where yours has got to.

Your email and your relationship to the incident are never shown publicly, and the person named in an entry cannot see who reported them. If they believe an entry is wrong, they can [appeal](/appeals), and a moderator other than the one who approved it reviews it within fourteen working days.

The full set of questions people ask before submitting is answered on the [about page](/about).

## Why bother

Because the comment outlives the moment it was written in, and because the person who wrote it usually does not expect it to.

A conviction takes [three and a half years on average](/blog/180-days-in-law-three-years-in-practice). A comment takes nine seconds. The asymmetry between those two numbers is most of what this archive is about: the public reaction to gender violence moves at a speed the justice system cannot match, shapes what survivors expect before they ever reach a police station, and leaves almost no durable record of itself.

Daag is a record, not a verdict and not a punishment. It takes no position on guilt in any criminal matter, publishes no private data, and asks that entries not be used to harass anyone. You can [read the archive](/archive), [search a name or profile link](/search), or [submit something you have seen](/submit).

---

*Daag is a public archive, not a law firm, and nothing here is legal advice. If you are in danger now, call 999. For the national women and children helpline, call 109. For online harassment and blackmail, Police Cyber Support for Women is on 01320-000888.*

# Where to report online abuse in Bangladesh, and what happens next

> The numbers that work, what the 2026 ordinance changed, what each route can and cannot do, and how to keep evidence that survives a deleted post.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/where-to-report-online-abuse-in-bangladesh

Most online abuse in Bangladesh is never reported to anyone. ActionAid found that **85 percent** of women who had experienced violence online never complained ([Prothom Alo, 27 November 2022](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/p5uqt9qjl3)), and of everyone recorded as a victim of cyber violence in the first half of 2025, **97 percent were women and children** ([Prothom Alo, 9 July 2025](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/7gdiyso4ho)).

Part of that is the well-founded belief that nothing will come of it. Part of it is simply not knowing where to go.

This is the practical version. What exists, what each route is actually for, and what to do first.

## Do this before anything else

Evidence is the thing most complaints lack, and it is the thing that disappears fastest. Before reporting, before replying, before blocking:

1. **Screenshot everything**, showing the content, the account name, and the surrounding thread. Not a crop of the words.
2. **Copy the link to the post or comment**, and separately the link to the account's profile.
3. **Note the date and time** you captured it.
4. **Do not edit the images.** No cropping out timestamps, no highlighting. An altered screenshot cannot be verified by anyone.
5. **Only then block or report** to the platform. Blocking can remove your own access to the evidence.

A deleted post is not recoverable by you, and usually not by the police either. Whatever you did not capture is gone.

## The numbers

| Who | Number | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| National emergency | **999** | Immediate physical danger. Police, fire, ambulance. Open all hours |
| Women and children helpline | **109** | Government helpline for violence against women and children. Free, all hours |
| Child helpline | **1098** | For anyone under 18 |
| Police Cyber Support for Women | **01320-000888** | Online harassment, blackmail, image abuse. Staffed for women complainants |
| National legal aid | **16430** | Free legal advice, office hours |
| Online complaint | [cybercrime.gov.bd](https://cybercrime.gov.bd) | Written report, if you would rather not call |

If there is any threat to your physical safety, 999 comes first and everything else can wait.

## What changed in 2026

In January the government approved two ordinances covering harassment, and the detail that matters here is the scope: the protections explicitly bring **sexual harassment through social media, email, messaging platforms and other digital technologies** within their purview, rather than leaving online conduct in a gap ([The Daily Star, 30 January 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/crime-justice/news/two-ordinances-protect-women-kids-all-spaces-4094071)).

The same reporting describes a requirement, following a writ petition, that every workplace and institution form a **five-member harassment complaint committee headed by a woman**, and that the guidelines are to be treated as law until legislation is made.

Two practical consequences:

- If the harassment came from a colleague or a classmate, there is supposed to be an internal committee with a woman at its head, and it is supposed to investigate. You can ask for it by name.
- Online conduct is no longer easily dismissed as outside the rules.

This is a change on paper. The Daily Star has documented the gaps between the legal framework and enforcement in practice ([17 December 2025](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/gaps-laws-enforcement-fuel-cyber-violence-against-women-4061176)), and nothing here should be read as a promise that a complaint will be acted on.

## What each route can actually do

Being honest about this saves people from the second disappointment.

**The police, including cyber support.** Can investigate, can require platforms to act in some circumstances, and can bring a prosecution. Slow, and dependent on the officer in front of you. Bring your evidence printed or on a device you can hand over, and keep your own copy.

**The platform.** Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and the rest can remove content and suspend accounts, which is often the fastest relief. They cannot give you any remedy beyond that, and removal destroys the evidence unless you captured it first.

**A workplace or institution committee.** Can discipline someone inside the institution. Cannot act on a stranger.

**Legal aid.** Can advise on whether what happened fits an offence, which is genuinely hard to judge from outside.

**Daag.** Keeps a public, verified record of what was written. It is not a complaint, it does not reach the police, and it produces no legal consequence. What it does is make the statement durable, searchable and attributable after the original is deleted.

Those are different tools. Using the archive is not a substitute for reporting to anyone, and reporting to the police does not preserve the public record.

## If you want it in the archive

[Submit it here](/submit). You will need the link to the commenter's profile, the link to the source post, and an unedited screenshot. Typing out the comment is optional and is what makes the entry findable later.

Nothing is published automatically. A moderator opens the links, checks the screenshot has not been altered, settles the category, and then approves, rejects, or asks for more, usually within three to five working days. You get a reference number to check the status.

Your email and your relationship to the incident are never published, and the person named cannot see who reported them. Anyone named can [appeal](/appeals), and a moderator other than the one who approved it reviews the evidence within fourteen working days.

More on how all of this works, including the questions people ask most often, is on the [about page](/about).

## One thing worth knowing

The comment you are looking at now will probably be deleted. That is the ordinary life cycle of this material: it is written in public, it does its work, and it is removed when the story stops trending or when its author thinks better of it.

Whether or not you report it anywhere, capture it now. Deciding later what to do with a screenshot is possible. Recovering a screenshot you never took is not.

---

**Sources.** Prothom Alo for the ActionAid research and the cyber violence figures; The Daily Star for the January 2026 ordinances and for the reporting on enforcement gaps. Helpline numbers are those published on daag-bd.com and are listed on the [contact page](/contact).

*Daag is a public archive, not a law firm, and nothing here is legal advice. If you are in danger now, call 999.*

# Who the accused usually is, according to this year's verdicts

> An imam, a stepfather, a neighbour, a teacher, a driver. Read the 2026 convictions together and the stranger is the exception, not the rule.
>
> Source: https://www.daag-bd.com/blog/who-the-accused-usually-is

Advice about keeping girls safe in Bangladesh tends to concentrate on strangers, darkness and distance. Do not go out late. Do not travel alone. Do not trust people you do not know.

Read this year's convictions together and that advice is aimed at the wrong place.

## The 2026 verdicts, side by side

| Verdict | Who the accused was | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Life term for raping a 15-year-old student in Jamalpur | **An imam** of a mosque, who taught her | [26 Oct 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/imam-gets-life-term-over-rape-girl-4307536) |
| Death sentence for raping a 13-year-old in Dhaka | **Her stepfather** | [29 Sep 2026](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/crime/7abjonw82b) |
| Life until death for raping a child in Chattogram | **A neighbour** | [Prothom Alo](https://www.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/district/jsgxcm9x4y) |
| Life term for raping a 15-year-old in Gopalganj | **A man known to her**, who threatened her | [15 Oct 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/man-gets-life-sentence-raping-15-year-old-girl-gopalganj-4299456) |
| Death and life terms over a gang rape at the MC College hostel in Sylhet | **Men at the institution** she was visiting | [14 Jul 2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/crime-justice/news/one-sentenced-death-three-life-term-impsonement-gang-rape-mc-college-4223566) |

In the Jamalpur case the prosecution described offences committed in late 2020 after the accused lured the girl with a promise of marriage. In Gopalganj, the case statement describes a man who took the girl to an isolated spot after threatening her.

The pattern is not subtle. An imam, a stepfather, a neighbour, a man known to the victim, men inside an institution. In most of these the accused had access because he was trusted, or because trust was not required: he was simply already there.

## The exceptions prove the shape

Two of the year's most reported cases do involve someone the victim did not know.

The [Cumilla case](/blog/what-a-confession-does-not-settle) involved an auto-rickshaw driver the girl hired. The [Tangail case](/blog/180-days-in-law-three-years-in-practice), in which three men received life terms, involved a woman travelling on a bus.

These are real and they are serious. They are also the cases that get the most coverage, which is part of why public understanding is skewed towards them. A stranger attacking a woman in transit is a story with a clear villain and an obvious lesson. A stepfather is a story with no lesson that anyone wants to hear.

## Why the misdirection is costly

If the danger is imagined as external, then safety is imagined as restriction. Stay in, come home early, do not travel alone, do not go to that place.

Every one of those measures is useless against an imam who teaches you, a stepfather in your house, or a neighbour on your lane. Worse, each of them increases the time a girl spends in the settings where the convictions above actually happened.

It also shapes what happens after. When the accused is known to the family, reporting means accusing someone the household depends on, lives beside, or answers to. That is a large part of why cases take as long as they do, and why so many never start. The [three years and seven months](/blog/180-days-in-law-three-years-in-practice) a case takes on average is not only a court backlog; it is also the time it takes for a family to decide, and to keep deciding, to continue.

## What the comments do with it

This is where Daag's record begins.

When the accused is a stranger, the comment section is mostly about punishment. When the accused is known to the victim, something different happens: the family comes under examination. Why did the mother not know, why was the child left there, why did they not move, what kind of household is this.

The archive contains both responses. The second is more corrosive, because it arrives when the family is already deciding whether pursuing the case is survivable.

## A caution about this reading

These are five reported verdicts, not a dataset. They were selected because they were reported in 2026 and the relationship between accused and victim was stated in the reporting; the full picture would require court records across all ninety-nine tribunals rather than the cases that reached a newspaper.

What can be said honestly is narrower than a statistic and still worth saying: in the convictions reported this year where the relationship is known, the accused was overwhelmingly someone the victim already knew. Any safety advice built on the opposite assumption is pointed away from where the evidence is.


## Where Daag fits

Daag does not investigate incidents and takes no position on guilt. It keeps [a record of what gets written publicly](/archive) underneath reporting like this, with a screenshot, a source link and a category, reviewed by a person before publication.

If you have seen a comment of that kind, you can [submit it](/submit). If an entry names you and is wrong, [appeal it](/appeals) and a different moderator will review the evidence within fourteen working days.

---

**Sources.** The Daily Star and Prothom Alo for each verdict, linked individually in the table above. Relationship descriptions are taken from the reporting, which in most cases is itself quoting a prosecutor or a case statement.

*Daag is a public archive, not a law firm, and nothing here is legal advice. For urgent help call 999. The child helpline is 1098 and the national women and children helpline is 109.*
